C was originally designed as a 'high-level assembler' providing a close-to-machine language for systems programming.
ISO C has evolved over nearly 40 years, adding features that emphasize conventional programming language attributes.
Most major commercial OS kernels are written in non-ISO dialects of C or rely on compiler-specific extensions.
ISO C's strict aliasing rules prevent certain common OS programming idioms involving pointer aliasing.
Undefined behavior in ISO C allows compilers to assume certain code paths never occur, enabling aggressive optimizations.
Compiler optimizations based on undefined behavior can silently remove or reorder code critical to OS correctness.
Dennis Ritchie criticized the ANSI C standard for creating a language unusable for real programs due to aliasing restrictions.
ISO C delegates many semantic decisions to the compiler rather than the machine or programmer.
Effective type rules in ISO C restrict how memory objects can be accessed and cast, complicating low-level programming.
Pointer equality in ISO C considers provenance, not just address, leading to surprising compiler optimizations.
Arithmetic overflow for signed integers is undefined behavior in ISO C, causing potential incorrect optimizations.
Implementations of malloc/free in ISO C require special rules to avoid undefined behavior.
Operating system code often disables strict aliasing optimizations in compilers like gcc to maintain correctness.
There is no general escape mechanism in ISO C to override aliasing rules without harming modularity.
Undefined behavior creates 'time bombs' that can unpredictably break large-scale applications.
ISO C's memory and pointer models are under active study and revision proposals in the WG14 committee.
Compiler optimizations relying on undefined behavior may produce different code behavior across compiler versions.
The paper provides examples from Linux kernel development illustrating practical problems caused by ISO C rules.
The ISO C standard's approach contrasts with K&R C, which gave more control to programmers and the machine.
The complexity and ambiguity of ISO C's undefined behavior and aliasing rules mystify many programmers.
